summary: Defines a way for mail senders to report on successes and failures when trying to set up encrypted SMTP connections using STARTTLS, DANE or MTA-STS. Reports help domain owners spot misconfiguration or attacks that cause undelivered or unprotected mail.

plainLanguage.summary: When a mail truck cannot use the safe tunnel, it sends a note saying so. This lets receivers read those notes and fix problems.

questions: how to set up tlsrpt record
subtitle: How mail senders tell recipient domains when encrypted delivery worked, failed, or was attacked.

tldr.problem: SMTP encryption with STARTTLS is opportunistic, so misconfiguration or an active attack can silently leave mail unencrypted or undelivered, and the receiving domain often cannot tell.
tldr.mechanism: A recipient domain publishes a TXT record at _smtp._tls saying where to send reports. Sending MTAs then deliver daily JSON reports, by email or HTTPS POST, with success and failure counts per policy and typed failure reasons.
tldr.outcome: Domain owners can spot attacks and diagnose misconfigurations for STARTTLS, DANE and MTA-STS, and the reports also act as a heartbeat showing TLS is working.

today: RFC 8460 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the companion reporting specification to RFC 8461 (MTA-STS) and is usable with DANE as in RFC 7672.

sections.title: Why TLS Reporting Exists
sections.content:
The STARTTLS extension (RFC 3207) lets SMTP servers upgrade a session to TLS. It follows the approach called Opportunistic Security (RFC 7435), which keeps working with clients that do not support STARTTLS. The cost is that an attacker could still eavesdrop. A downgrade or interception attack might delete parts of the session, such as the 250 STARTTLS response, or redirect it by overwriting the resolved MX record.

Such attacks are not necessarily apparent to the receiving MTA, so this RFC defines a way for sending domains to report failures at several stages of the MTA-to-MTA conversation. It covers failures in routing, DNS resolution and STARTTLS negotiation, plus policy validation errors for DANE (RFC 6698) and MTA-STS (RFC 8461). It is a companion to MTA-STS and adds reporting for those using DANE (RFC 7672).

Reports can also serve as a heartbeat showing that sessions are negotiating TLS as expected.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail trucks try to use a safe tunnel, but a bad guy might block it or the tunnel might be broken. This gives trucks a way to tell the receiver about problems.

sections.title: Publishing a Reporting Policy
sections.content:
A domain asks for reports by publishing a DNS TXT record under the name _smtp._tls, similar to DMARC policies. For the Policy Domain example.com, the policy is read from _smtp._tls.example.com. The record has a version, v=TLSRPTv1, and a required rua field listing one or more comma-separated URIs. Two schemes are supported: mailto and https.

If several TXT records come back, those not starting with v=TLSRPTv1; are discarded. If the number left is not one, senders MUST assume the domain does not implement TLSRPT. Unknown fields in a syntactically valid record are ignored.

For https, reports are submitted with POST, and submitters MAY ignore certificate validation errors. For mailto, the sender MUST deliver the report despite any TLS-related failures, which may mean unencrypted delivery, and SHOULD NOT include that session in the next report. Emailed reports MUST carry a valid DKIM signature by the reporting domain, and reports lacking one MUST be ignored. The signature MUST NOT use the l= attribute, so an attacker cannot append misleading data.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain puts up a sign in the phone book saying 'send your notes about my mail to this address'. Senders look up the sign before they report.

sections.title: The JSON Report
sections.content:
A report is a plaintext file in the Internet JSON (I-JSON) format. It holds report metadata (organization name, contact address, a unique report id, and the date range), then an array of policies. The array is required even when only one policy applied, since a sender may report several, for example an MTA-STS policy and a DANE record for the same domain and MX.

Each policy entry has a policy block (type, policy string, policy domain and MX host), a summary with total-successful-session-count and total-failure-session-count, and a failure-details array. The policy-type is tlsa, sts, or the literal no-policy-found. Each failure detail names the result-type, the sending MTA IP, the receiving MX hostname and IP, a failed-session-count, and optionally an HELO string, an additional-information URI and a failure-reason-code.

Failure types are not exclusive, so one send attempt with several errors may be counted under several types. Internationalized domain names MUST appear as Punycode A-labels. A report SHOULD cover a full UTC day, 00:00 to 24:00, and should be sent after a delay so receivers are not overloaded; the RFC's example uses a random delay of up to four hours.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is a tidy form: who is writing, which day it covers, how many deliveries went fine, how many failed, and why each failure happened.

sections.title: Result Types
sections.content:
The initial set of result types is expected to grow with experience. It has three groups.

  • Negotiation failures: starttls-not-supported, certificate-host-mismatch, certificate-expired, certificate-not-trusted and the catch-all validation-failure.
  • DANE failures: tlsa-invalid, dnssec-invalid and dane-required.
  • MTA-STS failures: sts-policy-fetch-error, sts-policy-invalid and sts-webpki-invalid.

For certificate-not-trusted and validation-failure, the reporter SHOULD add a failure-reason-code with a short error code or text, such as X509_V_ERR_UNHANDLED_CRITICAL_CRL_EXTENSION. Transient errors from busy networks or TCP timeouts are not required to be reported.
sections.plainLanguage: Each failure gets a name tag, like 'tunnel missing', 'ID card expired' or 'ID card is for someone else', so the receiver knows what to fix.

sections.title: Delivering Reports
sections.content:
Reports go by email or by HTTPS POST, and SHOULD be compressed with gzip. The RFC notes that skipping compression can make a report too large for a receiver, with ten megabytes a commonly observed limit. The filename is RECOMMENDED to follow sender!policy-domain!begin-timestamp!end-timestamp[!unique-id].json, or .json.gz if compressed.

An emailed report uses the multipart/report type with report-type="tlsrpt". It has a human-readable first part and a machine-readable second part of type application/tlsrpt+json, or application/tlsrpt+gzip if compressed. Two new header fields MUST be included, TLS-Report-Domain and TLS-Report-Submitter, and the submitter must match the domain of the report's contact address. When sending failure reports by SMTP, Sending MTAs MUST NOT honor MTA-STS or DANE TLSA failures.

For HTTPS, the receiver MUST return a successful response, typically 200 or 201. A sender SHOULD retry a failed delivery for up to 24 hours, ideally with exponential backoff. If the subject or filename disagrees with the report body, the body is authoritative.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is zipped up to keep it small and handed over by mail or by dropping it at the receiver's door. If nobody answers, the sender tries again for a day.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists risks created by the reporting channel itself.

  • Flooding of the report endpoint could blind a domain to an ongoing attack.
  • Untrusted content: reports could carry malicious data, so implementers should not evaluate their contents carelessly.
  • Report snooping with a bogus TLSRPT record is judged not a significant new vulnerability, since an attacker who can poison DNS can already learn more.
  • Ignoring HTTPS validation is allowed because a misconfigured SMTP server often means a misconfigured HTTPS server, and the RFC judges the risk of missed reports to outweigh the risk of interception.
  • Reports as DDoS: report destinations may be outside the Policy Domain, which could be abused to flood a victim, though the risk is lower than for DMARC.

An attacker able to downgrade a connection may also block discovery of the TLSRPT record. Administrators are encouraged to use a large TTL on the record or deploy DNSSEC. On privacy, a report can reveal the sender's TLS implementation, and indirectly its operating system or region.
sections.plainLanguage: The note system could itself be abused, by flooding the mailbox with junk or hiding bad news. The RFC lists these dangers and ways to reduce them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the message header fields TLS-Report-Domain and TLS-Report-Submitter, and created a Report Type Registry for the report-type parameter of multipart/report (Specification Required) with tlsrpt as an initial entry. It also registered the +gzip media type suffix and the media types application/tlsrpt+json and application/tlsrpt+gzip. Finally it created the STARTTLS Validation Result Types registry, holding the result types above, where new entries use Expert Review.
sections.plainLanguage: New names the RFC invents get written in the official lists so nobody else uses them for something different.
